senses.sense_definition: A temporary departure from the main subject in speech or writing.

examples.text: The lectures included lengthy <w>digressions</w> on topics ranging from the professor's dog to the meaning of life.
After a brief <w>digression</w> about his childhood, the speaker returned to the main point of the presentation.

senses.sense_definition: The deliberate act of straying from the main theme in discourse or rhetoric, especially for stylistic effect.

examples.text: The author employed rhetorical <w>digression</w> to entertain the reader while developing background context.
In classical oratory, a well-placed <w>digression</w> can effectively capture the interest of the audience.

senses.sense_definition: A physical turning aside or wandering away from a designated path or route.

examples.text: Their brief <w>digression</w> from the marked trail led them toward an unexpected mountain stream.
By this little <w>digression</w> into the countryside, the travelers managed to avoid the crowded main road.

traits.comment: Rarely used for physical movement in modern English

senses.sense_definition: An act of straying from standard conduct, virtue, or an established rule; a moral deviation or error.

examples.text: The strict moral code of the community allowed no room for any ethical <w>digression</w>.
He viewed every minor violation of the rules as a serious <w>digression</w> from proper order.

traits.comment: Used in archaic or historical contexts

senses.sense_definition: A deflection, deviation, or angular distance from a normal position or calculated orbit.

examples.text: Early astronomers carefully observed the celestial <w>digression</w> of the planet from its anticipated path.
The calculated <w>digression</w> of the body was greatest near the time of the solstice.
